quote: Rational agents make decisions that maximize the probabilistic expectation of a coherent utility function
content: The essay does not offer the axioms as a neutral vantage point. Two paragraphs later it says the exact rules of decision theory "are called into question by, e.g., Newcomblike problems," and it refuses to settle such disputes by definition. What it does claim is that experimental psychologists use probability and decision theory as their gold standards, and that is a description of the field. The case for the axioms is not that nobody contests them. It is that departing from them has a cost: an agent that violates independence can be led into dynamic inconsistency, choosing plans it will later abandon, or into paying to avoid free information, which breaks the value-of-information result the Fable pass relies on elsewhere (Good 1967; Wakker 1988, Journal of Behavioral Decision Making). Buchak's risk-weighted agents accept that cost, which makes it a price they pay, not a refutation of the axioms. Aumann's 1962 paper drops completeness and still recovers a utility function that respects every preference the agent does have (Aumann 1962); incompleteness models indecision, not a rival standard.

quote: No one can actually calculate and obey the math, any more than you can predict the stock market by calculating the movements of quarks.
content: The essay does ask the question. The next paragraph answers it: the whole site exists because "there's a whole further art to finding the truth and accomplishing value from inside a human mind." The ecological-rationality programme is an ally of that art, not a rival, because it scores heuristics by out-of-sample predictive accuracy, which is the essay's own norm of a map that reflects the territory. Gigerenzer and Brighton explain why take-the-best beats regression on small samples by appeal to the bias–variance decomposition, a theorem of statistical estimation (Gigerenzer & Brighton 2009). When a heuristic wins because the full model overfits, the full model was the wrong prior for that problem, and the heuristic is doing better inference by the same standard. That is the norm vindicated, not an exception to it.

quote: the judgment that P(Bill plays jazz) is less than P(Bill plays jazz, Bill is an accountant) is labeled incorrect
content: The frequency results are real, but they cannot carry the weight put on them. Tversky and Kahneman ran frequency versions themselves in 1983 and reported that the fallacy shrank without disappearing (Tversky & Kahneman 1983). When the meaning of "probable" is taken out of dispute by having subjects bet money on which statement will turn out true, the conjunction fallacy persists (Sides, Osherson, Bonini & Viale 2002), and a subject placing a bet is not reading "probable" as "typical." Tentori, Bonini and Osherson (2004, Cognitive Science) likewise found that frequency formats reduce the error without eliminating it. The label "incorrect" attaches to the judgment people will stake money on, which is the one that matters.
